A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent attempt by one of the pilots to seize control of the aircraft and crash it, passengers and Israeli officials said.
"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers and other crew members who intervened. The prime minister said he instructed Israel's "security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats."
An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack, which was thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist, and with their own hands returned control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew that was present," according to a statement.
The plane diverted to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base. No passengers were injured in the incident, but the pilot who was attacked by his fellow crew member reportedly sustained stab wounds, and Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
According to Netanyahu, the pilot who carried out the stabbing was placed under arrest and was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities." An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship.
In a social media post , the Israel Foreign Ministry identified the wounded pilot as Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. It described him as a "hero" who "fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit."
According to the foreign ministry, Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door to allow passengers and crew to enter and intervene.
"Together, their extraordinary courage saved 174 lives," the foreign ministry said.
The plane landed in Tel Aviv shortly before 8 p.m. local time on Wednesday. People could be heard singing and chanting as the passengers disembarked. Family members came to the airport to celebrate their loved ones' safe return.
One passenger said the plane dropped "very, very sharply suddenly" multiple times before balancing out. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."
"There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," Ohayon said.
Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
One passenger seated at the front of the plane said a "group of young people fought" with the attacker.
The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information. CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.
The Israeli Air Force was first to notice something was wrong, an Israeli official with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News. The air force noticed the flight deviating from its flight path and descending at an alarming rate, the official said. When it tried to contact the plane, it received no response. It then got the emergency alert that specified a hijacking, not just a distress call.
At that point, according to the official, the flight was still several hundred miles from Israeli airspace. However, even 90 seconds or so into the incident, the air force feared a 9/11-style attack, so it immediately made the decision to close Israeli airspace, and seconds after that it scrambled several jets, the official said.
The jets never left Israeli airspace because it became clear that the plane had turned toward Saudi Arabia, and that Saudi Arabia had scrambled its own jets, the official said.
This sequence of events occurred within the span of about two to three minutes, according to the official, and the entire episode lasted about 15 minutes.
A statement from FlyDubai said only that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and that the aircraft "was successfully secured by on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely" in Saudi Arabia.
The airline said "all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for," and it confirmed that two replacement aircraft had been deployed to Tabuk to "relieve the passengers and crew," though many Israeli passengers told media outlets they would not reboard a FlyDubai plane.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the airline said in its statement, urging "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that there were four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship aboard the flight.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.
Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.
Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."
Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in the upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X : "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."
"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday , saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."
"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

articles.title_orig: FCC head says government-funded Trump ads are ‘normal’ and ‘don’t raise any red flags’
articles.title_zh: FCC head says government-funded Trump ads are ‘normal’ and ‘don’t raise any red flags’
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Supreme Court rules Tennessee can execute lone woman on death row
Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday that new pro-Trump TV ads paid for with government funds don’t “merit any sort of FCC review.”
“It doesn’t strike me as anything at all out of the ordinary,” Carr said of the ads, which have aired across the country in recent weeks.
Asked about allegations that the ads are “propaganda,” Carr laughed.
The White House has “explained that these are just normal-course public service announcements, PSAs, that you see all the time. I don’t think there’s anything unique or different about it,” he said at a news conference .
“There’s nothing in there that strikes me that merit any sort of FCC review,” said Carr, whom Trump appointed to the agency.
A reporter pointed out that the progressive advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC noting that the Trump campaign used one of the ads in 2024.
Carr brushed off the concern, telling reporters that “there’s groups on the left that have, you know, long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process” but that the ads “don’t raise any red flags.”
Public Citizen did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC, told NBC News in a statement, “I recognize the concern shared by others that taxpayer dollars are being used to promote a political message, particularly given the timing of these ads coming so close to an election.”
“While it is not surprising to see the FCC exercise a double standard when it comes to its investigative decisions, I am certain we will hear more about this from folks in Congress, who are ultimately responsible,” her statement said.
The use of federal funds to pay for the ads has drawn bipartisan criticism , with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., saying they “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., calling them an “absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like.”
Trump defended the ads when asked about them Wednesday in the Oval Office.
“I’m not running for office and I don’t talk about anybody,” he said. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.”
“Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country,” he added.
The first of the ads features Trump describing how he wants to “defeat communism” while the song “ Love Me ” by JMSN plays in the background.
Another spot is a slightly shorter version of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, which shows him walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voice-over to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”
In its complaint Tuesday, Public Citizen said that the messages are thinly veiled campaign ads timed to motivate Trump’s supporters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and that they are unlawful.
“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising. Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads,” the complaint says, adding that none of the ads to date “meet the standard of a public service announcement.”
“They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program,” the complaint says.
Carr has made headlines for using his post to go after late-night comedians like Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and network programs that he has alleged have liberal biases.
The FCC issued an order this year directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated television stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule after the White House and ABC clashed over a joke Kimmel made about first lady Melania Trump.
Disney is challenging the review with a suit alleging the FCC is seeking to coerce and retaliate against “a network that refuses to bow to the ⁠administration’s ​demands.” Carr has said the ABC license review stems from the FCC’s probe of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices — not “speech.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Leaning into culture war flashpoints, Hegseth says he has transformed U.S. military
articles.title_zh: Leaning into culture war flashpoints, Hegseth says he has transformed U.S. military
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Wednesday in Quantico, Va. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
At a gathering at U.S. Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told hundreds of junior military officers and enlisted leaders that the Trump administration has achieved a cultural shift in the military.
"No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors," Hegseth said on Wednesday. "The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in, with testosterone testing on top."
Hegseth has vowed to shrink what he says is a bloated flag-officer corps since he took over at the Pentagon. He said he'd already achieved a 10% reduction and aimed to reach 20%. But his firings so far, and the unconventional way he has reached down into promotion boards to essentially end the careers of some senior officers, has drawn bipartisan criticism. Many of the notable firings were of Black or female officers, let go without explanation despite excellent service records.
Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, issued this statement:
"Throughout his tenure, Secretary Hegseth has taken countless reckless, partisan actions that have damaged our military. He has ended the careers of dozens of our most accomplished senior officers and refused to explain why. Today's news should alarm every American."
In his speech, Hegseth defended his policies and claimed that retention and recruitment, including among women and minorities, has risen. He called the new force "color-blind" and merit-based. Hegseth took considerable time to rail against the media for reporting on troop morale and depleted munitions stocks in the war with Iran.
"A free press is, of course, important, but partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually," he said.
Despite the war in Iran, now in its seventh month, the Pentagon hasn't held a news briefing since May, even with a handpicked press corps more sympathetic to the Trump administration.
The event echoed a gathering last year where Hegseth delivered an unusually partisan speech to hundreds of generals and admirals, despite the U.S. military's foundational tradition of avoiding politics. The flag officers stayed almost completely silent as Hegseth spoke about culture war issues mentioned in his book The War on Warriors . He said that the "State of the Force" address would be an annual event, and was no less partisan this year, blaming past generals and defense secretaries by name for weakening the military.
Hegseth also announced new initiatives around autonomous weapons, technological innovation, base construction and domestic production of essential military supplies.
He pledged to elevate the military's chaplains and called religious faith the most essential component of our republic.
This week Hegseth also announced an end to civilian tenured positions at U.S. military academies, which a Pentagon press release said would "reform our educational institutions to ensure they remain laser-focused on lethality and readiness."
While criticizing elite academic institutions as anti-American in his speech, Hegseth named five new colleges that will pilot an enhanced relationship with the Pentagon to produce officer candidates.

articles.title_orig: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.title_zh: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee can carry out its planned execution of the lone woman on death row after the Supreme Court vacated a lower court’s Wednesday morning order that had temporarily blocked the move.
The high court’s decision hours later caps a flurry of last-minute legal maneuvering in a bid by convicted murderer Christa Pike’s legal team to spare her life. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
About an hour before her scheduled execution at 10 a.m. local time in Nashville, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth District said it needed to review claims made by her lawyers. At issue was whether Pike can reopen a court proceeding centered around her allegations that she was sexually abused beginning when she was a child — abuse that the state did not dispute at a special hearing in August.
The appeals court in a split decision agreed to a “short” reprieve halting her execution “in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”
In turn, the state attorney general’s office asked the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that the execution must go on to “avoid rewarding Pike’s abusive delay tactics.”
Both Gov. Bill Lee and the Supreme Court had said this week they would not stop Pike’s execution.
Before learning Monday that Lee would not be intervening in her case, Pike, 50, wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser: “Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace.”
“I am not afraid to die,” wrote Pike, who has been on death row for more than three decades. “I’m only nervous about the process.”
If executed, Pike would be the first woman in more than 200 years that the state puts to death, according to historical records .
In 1995, Pike was 18 when Knoxville police say she and two teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19. Police say Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike doesn’t dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They had asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, will likely create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state hasn’t denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court appeared to be Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.” The high court denied her petition Tuesday evening.
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken” that the governor would not be granting clemency.
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
In her letter, Pike wrote that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also point to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time. Tadaryl Shipp received a life sentence because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and received probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention. Pike’s lawyers say that her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers say that her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed into solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, was asked by Pike’s lawyers to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider if any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse. Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. But, she added, Pike’s case is a lesson of the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.
May Martinez is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.
Martinez recalled how, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts weren’t buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. articles.title_orig: Live updates: California’s gubernatorial candidates debate ahead of midterms | CNN Politics
articles.title_zh: Live updates: California’s gubernatorial candidates debate ahead of midterms | CNN Politics
articles.content_orig:
The candidates  trade personal jabs and spar over policy differences on affordability, AI and immigration.
• A heated debate took place tonight between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who are vying to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom as the next California governor. The candidates sparred on a range of topics, including immigration , affordability and how they would address the impact of AI.
• However, the policies of President Donald Trump and, to a lesser extent, Newsom underpinned most of the debate. Becerra tied Hilton to the president at every possible opportunity as the Republican candidate sought to avoid being linked too closely to Trump while blaming Democrats who have full control of California’s government for the state’s woes.
Closing tonight’s debate, both candidates were asked about the lessons they’d take from California’s 176-year history on the anniversary of its founding this month.
But the Republican repeated his argument that Democrats had mismanaged the state, and that rival Xavier Becerra did not deserve a chance to extend his party’s control of the governor’s office.
“That spirit is being crushed by this bloated nanny-state bureaucratic government that Xavier has been a part of for 36 years and would continue. It’s time to try something different,” Hilton said.
Becerra, meanwhile, said California fulfilled the promise of the American dream “more than in any other place in the country. California has thrived. Our dynamism has made us the fourth largest economy in the world.”
He also pointed to his parent’s foundational immigrant experience.
Former US Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra stressed his support for vaccines amid the country’s recent rising measles cases .
“That’s what happens when vaccine-deniers take over,” the Democrat told CNN’s Dana Bash and Jake Tapper tonight.
“And this is what will happen to California if you let someone who is willing to promote that type of attitude become governor of the state of California,” Becerra said. “We can’t reward those who are willing to let families die.”
His, Republican Steve Hilton, also said that he was “pro-vaccine” but suggested that lowering the number of requirements would help increase compliance for “vaccines that are really important for public health.”
Some context: During the Covid-19 pandemic, Becerra was criticized for maintaining a lower profile. Administration officials who were in meetings and virtual calls with the secretary at the time say he took a conflict-averse approach in dealing with the administration’s other Covid-19 leaders. Still, his department coordinated the undertaking of distributing vaccines to hundreds of millions of Americans.
CNN’s Elise Hammond contributed reporting.
Republican Steve Hilton criticized the Democratic Party’s education policy for spending “nearly the highest amount in the entire country for some of the worst results” in California, portraying his opponent Xavier Becerra as a candidate who would do more of the same.
Jumping on that, Becerra said Hilton doesn’t like teachers.
“I believe that the people who are supposed to train our kids should be treated like professionals. They are underpaid compared to professionals with similar education levels,” Becerra said, adding that they should be treated “like real professionals.”
Becerra blamed California’s school problems on too many compliance requirements.
“Before we pass a child on, we’re making sure that they are at grade level. We have to provide the tutoring that they need. We have to start earlier. We’ve started transitional kindergarten, which gets a 4-year-old into our schools. But too often when they’re one, two and three years of age, they’re not being prepared to get into our school system. So I would fight to make sure that we’re working with our teachers because they’re the most important people that will make sure their success for this child,” Becerra said, adding he’ll make sure taxpayer dollars go to public schools.
The candidates running to be California’s next governor outlined what they would do to keep film and television production in the state.
This year is on track to become one of the slowest years on record for production and small businesses in California, and workers in the TV and movie industry are struggling to find jobs.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, stressed the importance of these jobs the entertainment industry provides.
Last week, another group of bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced a 20% tax credit bill in a bid to bring production back to California.
Steve Hilton, a Republican, sought to blame Democrats who have been running the state for bringing the industry to the “brink of collapse.”
Republican Steve Hilton said that he has confidence in California’s election systems when asked about President Donald Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud.
“I’ve got confidence in what we saw in the primary and in this process,” Hilton, whom Trump has endorsed, said.
But he seized on remarks from Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who recently joked that “we don’t need an election on November 3” because of her high confidence in Democrats’ retaining control of the governor’s office.
“That is the attitude we get from these people who’ve been in charge of our state for 16 years, and they think that they can just do whatever they want, get whatever bad results, the highest taxes in the country for the worst results, taking everybody for granted, taking their votes for granted,” Hilton said.
Becerra, meanwhile, criticized Hilton for backing Proposition 39, an initiative on the ballot this year that would require voters to present a government-issued ID to cast a ballot in person.
“That would make it harder for Californians to vote,”  Becerra said of the measure. “We have to all vote no on 39 to send a clear message to Donald Trump and Steve Hilton that we want people to vote.”
Hilton argued back that “there’s a majority in this state who agree that it’s reasonable to show ID when you vote,” and echoed the refrain that “if we vote the same way in this state as we’ve been doing, we’re going to get the same results.”
Xavier Becerra reiterated his position of not backing the one-time wealth tax on billionaires this November, even though a majority of California Democrats support it.
He said the proposal “is not the way to do tax policy,” before touting his experience enacting various tax cuts during his time in politics.

articles.title_orig: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says
articles.title_zh: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, Burnham says
articles.content_orig:
The government believes that Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC. He did not provide further details.
Iran has responded, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the UK leader was "barking up the wrong tree".
"I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all," he wrote on social media.
Asked why the suspects had been released on bail - a decision which has been openly questioned by President Donald Trump - Burnham insisted the men were subject to the "strictest possible bail conditions".
Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said: "I will tell you, I would have said, 'don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."
But Burnham said: "I think people need to understand that when it says released - that isn't as people might think. It's obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions.
"The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that."
Burnham's comments come after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor" .
In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally".
Burnham said that the government had been "talking to our counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done", and that he had "complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this".
"We will say more in due course but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part," he told the BBC.
"Of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham added.
Burnham's comments came after it emerged that one of the five men had dialled 999 himself before the group were arrested.
The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base.
They are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.
The men were released on bail in what police described as an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.
The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Before Araghchi's comments the Iranian embassy in London had said it rejected "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the latest incident.

So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 100 million income tax returns for 2022.
That means tens of millions of households have yet to file their returns. If yours is among them, here are some last-minute tax-filing tips to keep in mind as the Tuesday, April 18 deadline approaches.
Not everyone has to file on April 18: If you live in a federally declared disaster area, have a business there — or have relevant tax documents stored by businesses in that area — it’s likely the IRS has already extended the filing and payment deadlines for you. Here is where you can find the specific extension dates for each disaster area.
Thanks to many rounds of extreme weather in recent months, for instance, tax filers in most of California — which accounts for 10% to 15% of all federal filers — have already been granted an extension until Oct. 16 to file and to pay, according to an IRS spokesperson.
If you’re in the armed forces and are currently or were recently stationed in a combat zone, the filing and payment deadlines for your 2022 taxes are most likely extended by 180 days. But your specific extended filing and payment deadlines will depend on the day you leave (or left) the combat zone. This IRS publication offers more detail.
Taxes and adulting: What to know about filing taxes on your own for the first time
Lastly, if you made little to no money last year (typically less than $12,950 for single filers and $25,900 for married couples), you may not be required to file a return. But you may want to anyway if you think you are eligible for a refund thanks to, for instance, refundable tax credits such as the Earned Income Tax Credit . (Use this IRS tool to gauge whether you are required to file this year.) You also are likely eligible to use IRS Free File (intended for those with adjusted gross income of $73,000 or less) so it won’t cost you to submit a return.
Your paycheck may not be your only source of income: If you had one full-time job you may think that is the only income you made and have to report. But that’s not necessarily so.
Other potentially taxable and reportable income sources include:
Organize your tax documents: By now you should have received every tax document that third parties are required to send you (your employer, bank, brokerage, etc.).
If you don’t recall receiving a hard copy of a tax form in the mail, check your email and your online accounts — a document may have been sent to you electronically.
Here are some of the tax forms you may have received:
“Be aware that there’s no form for some taxable income, like proceeds from renting out your vacation property, meaning you’re responsible for reporting it on your own,” according to the Illinois CPA Society.
One very last-minute way to reduce your 2022 tax bill: If you’re eligible to make a tax-deductible contribution to an IRA and haven’t done so for last year, you have until April 18 to contribute up to $6,000 ($7,000 if you’re 50 or older). That will reduce your tax bill and augment your retirement savings.
Proofread your return before submitting it: Do this whether you’re using tax software or working with a professional tax preparer .
Little mistakes and oversights delay the processing of your return (and the issuance of your refund if you’re owed one). You want to avoid things like having a typo in your name, birth date, Social Security number or direct deposit number; choosing the wrong filing status (e.g., married vs single); making a simple math error; or leaving a required field blank.
What to do if you can’t file by April 18: If you’re not able to file by next Tuesday, fill out Form 4868 electronically or on paper and send it in by April 18. You will be granted an automatic six-month extension to file.
Your tax refund may be smaller this year. Here's why
Note, however, that an extension to file is not an extension to pay. You will be charged interest (currently running at 7%) and a penalty on any amount you still owe for 2022 but haven’t paid by April 18.
So if you suspect you still owe tax — perhaps you had some income outside of your job for which tax wasn’t withheld or you had a big capital gain last year — approximate how much more you owe and send that money to the IRS by Tuesday.
You can choose to do so by mail, attaching a check to your extension request form. Make sure your envelope is postmarked no later than April 18.
Or the more efficient route is pay what you owe electronically at IRS.gov, said CPA Damien Martin, a tax partner at EY. If you do that, the IRS notes you will not have to file a Form 4868. “The IRS will automatically process an extension of time to file,” the agency notes in its instructions.
If you opt to electronically pay directly from your bank account, which is free, select “extension” and then “tax year 2022” when given the option.
You can also pay by credit or debit card, but you will be charged a processing fee . Doing so, though, may become much more costly than just a fee if you charge your tax payment but don’t pay your credit card bill off in full every month, since you likely pay a high interest rate on outstanding balances.
If you still owe income taxes to your state, remember that you may need to go through a similar exercise of filing for an extension and making a payment to your state’s revenue department, Martin said.
Use this interactive tax assistant for basic questions you may have: The IRS provides an “ interactive tax assistant ” that can help you answer more than 50 basic questions pertaining to your individual circumstance on income, deductions, credits and other technical questions.

Sean “Diddy” Combs’ release date has been moved up once again, just as reports of his alleged pampered federal prison lifestyle have emerged.
The 56-year-old is scheduled to be released on Jan. 21, 2028, from FCI Fort Dix, a low-security federal prison in New Jersey, according to the Federal Bureau of Prisons inmate database.
The disgraced music mogul was sentenced to 50 months in prison last October after he was convicted of transporting prostitutes across state lines for drug-fueled sex performances known as “freak-offs.”
The initial release date for Combs was projected for June 2028.
Imprisoned music mogul Sean Combs inches closer to his release from federal prison. His sentence has yet again been slightly reduced.
Time in the jailhouse for the “Mo Money Mo Problems” rapper has been shortened several times this year. The last update to his sentence occurred this summer, moving his release to late February 2028.
News of his shortened prison stint comes as reports of Combs’ special lifestyle have emerged in a report by NBC News published Tuesday.
According to four inmates — who were granted anonymity by the outlet to speak freely about life inside the prison — Combs has allegedly been paying men to clean and cook special meals for him, including curry chicken, pizza and empanadas, and that the hip-hop artist receives Chinese-style massages.
One man told NBC, “This is not some normal s— you see in jail. This is some rich s—. It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
The news outlet also reviewed footage obtained from inside the correctional facility, where Combs appeared to be using a contraband phone, which multiple inmates claim the artist-producer is using to scroll Instagram and view explicit nude content shared by an old girlfriend.
A jury found a onetime Compton gang leader guilty in the slaying of Tupac Shakur. The killing of Biggie Smalls, a.k.a. the Notorious B.I.G., remains unsolved.
There are also claims that the “I’ll Be Missing You” singer is purchasing an antidepressant drug known as Remeron, or “rem-roms,” from other inmates and that he keeps a secret stash of liquor that was smuggled into the prison by guards.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” one of the men told NBC. He recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
Sources also allege that individuals outside the prison are depositing thousands of dollars into the commissary accounts of those performing services for the “Bad Boy for Life” rapper.
A spokesperson for Combs responded to the Los Angeles Times’ request for comment.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said via email. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence within the rules and he patiently awaits the court’s decision on his appeal.”
Ivanna Ortiz, 36, was indicted on attempted murder and assault charges for allegedly opening fire on Rihanna’s home in March, according to court records made public Wednesday.
In an emailed statement to The Times, a FCI Fort Dix spokesperson said they cannot comment on the “conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual,” nor can they “confirm or deny the existence of a corresponding investigation.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson said. “Inmates are not permitted to have access to cell phones, and all incarcerated individuals in the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) who are found to violate the ‘Inmate Discipline Program’ policy are subject to sanctions.”
Combs’ legal troubles hit a peak last year after he was involved in a lengthy and public trial involving allegations of sexual assault and other violence. Among the accusers were his former girlfriend Casandra “Cassie” Ventura and producer Rodney “Lil Rod” Jones, who lodged civil complaints against the music tycoon.
In July 2025, Combs was found guilty on two counts of a prostitution-related charge, but the business titan was cleared of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking, which carried heavier penalties, including a maximum sentence of life in prison.

Arizona State University announced Wednesday it has put hockey coach Greg Powers on leave following the collapse of player Matthew Mayich during a summer team workout. Mayich, 21, remains on life support and is unlikely to recover, according to family attorney Rob Carey.
In response to the announcement, Carey said in an interview with NBC Nightly News that the family has said “since day one” that the entire coaching staff needed to be put on administrative leave. ASU has left in place another assistant coach who is good friends with the head coach “and that needs to change,” the attorney said.
“They did nothing right, literally nothing,” Carey said of the ASU coaching staff during the workout. “And as a result (of) what should have been a very preventable workout problem, heatstroke, a man is on life support and unlikely to come off of it,” he said.
“He’s incapacitated, and there’s almost no chance of recovery. But the family’s very devout, and they want to give their son a chance for a miracle,” Carey said.
ASU did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News on the family’s allegations and demands for an independent investigation.
But in its announcement on Powers’ leave, ASU Athletics Director Graham Rossini stated that the school’s “focus continues to be on Matthew and his family” and all student-athletes, to make sure they have “the support they need during this time and as the season begins.”
“We have continued to collect as much information as possible. After thorough and careful deliberation, I believe this is the best move to provide stability for the hockey program,” Rossini said.
Assistant Coach Mike Corbett will be leading the team this weekend for the season opener and an interim head coach would be named soon, according to the statement.
Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on Aug. 20. He suffered extreme heatstroke and has been hospitalized since his collapse.
Mayich’s parents, John and Christina Mayich, and seven other players from the hockey team called on Tuesday for coaches involved to be placed on leave and for an independent investigation.
The seven players, who did not share their names, submitted through their attorney a letter to ASU President Michael Crow  disputing the school’s account of what occurred.
In the letter, the players said they were afraid of being retaliated against because the coaches “decide our playing time, scholarship levels, and roster status.”
Although Carey said putting Powers on leave is a step in the right direction, he said there are players whose safety remains at risk and “retaliation is still possible.”
The athletes’ 26-page letter describes a workout session led by Tim Ziesel, an Army veteran and former Green Beret, on a day the afternoon high temperature was 104 degrees and the low was 74, according National Weather Service data. The players alleged in their letter that Zeisel left before Mayich collapsed.
According to the players, the workout did not include required emergency gear on site, including a tub of water for cooling off and a training plan had not been submitted to all the coaches.
In its report, ASU said temperatures were between 86 and 89 degrees during the workout, with relative humidity between 51% and 46%. The ASU report also stated that an athletic trainer evaluated Mayich’s condition, put cool water and iced towels on him and told him to stay down; he then called 911 and directed student-athletes to help move him to the shade.
Buddy Rake, Ziesel’s attorney, said Ziesel has offered to meet privately with Mayich’s family “and thinks a full and complete investigation should be done. “
“You have to find out what caused this. At the same time this workout is occurring, there’s probably 5,000 high school athletes in Arizona doing the same workout and nothing happens to them. So either the protocol is wrong, or there’s something else that happened,” Rake said.
The players’ letter alleges the university’s temperature and humidity figures “understate conditions on the field.”
The players noted that Mayich was new to Arizona, having been in the area for only eight days and having been involved in the hockey program for five. Drafted by the St. Louis Blues, Mayich is from Hamilton, Ontario, according to the NHL .
The players said that Mayich got no water during a break that lasted only seconds, because he was one of several players who did not reach the water on time before they were “pushed directly into the next task.”
The players said Powers characterized Mayich’s condition after his collapse as “just a little heat stroke” of the type he has seen before, according to their letter.
Carey said putting staff on leave and hiring an outside investigator is fundamental when things such as this occur.
In an interview with Canadian Broadcasting Company earlier this month, Mayich’s mother, Christina, said her son “was so excited to come to ASU — he said the facilities are even better live, because we watch it on YouTube and pictures and he just said it’s exciting.”
She said they’re taking her son’s situation “day by day.”
“Anybody who could send prayers for Matthew, it would be greatly appreciated because right now that’s what we need,” Christina Mayich said.

The Yankees are starting eight lefties for the first time in MLB postseason history.
The lineup for the Wild Card Series elimination game is set, and the Yankees are making headlines by starting eight left-handed hitters, not including switch-hitters, for the first time in MLB postseason history .
Ben Rice takes the leadoff spot after a record-breaking Game 1 performance against the Red Sox. He went 4-for-5 with two home runs, including an electrifying eighth-inning grand slam, and drove in six runs. It’s also worth noting that his fellow Massachusetts native Cam Schlittler also showed Boston no mercy, pitching six and a third scoreless innings with 10 strikeouts to completely shut down the offense.
Cody Bellinger, who went 1-for-4, will bat second followed by Luis García Jr. in the hole. He’ll start at first for Game 2 over Paul Goldschmidt, who went 0-for-3 with two walks and a run scored on Tuesday night. Spencer Jones will take the cleanup spot after going 1-for-3 with two runs scored and a walk in the Game 1 blowout win. He’ll be playing right field alongside Trent Grisham, who made his return in Game 1 after being reinstated from the IL.
Gleaming in his postseason debut, going 3-for-4 and scoring two runs, George Lombard Jr. is the perfect segue to cruise into the bottom of the order and the lone right-handed hitter in the starting nine. Jazz Chisholm Jr. will start at second over Anthony Volpe, who gave a promising performance in Game 1.
Grisham, who was sidelined most of September with a hamstring injury, is going back to his comfort zone at center and will take the seventh spot in the lineup. He’ll be followed by Austin Wells, who went 1-for-3 with two hits and identical RBIs on Tuesday night. Ryan McMahon will round out the order and start at third over Amed Rosario, who struck out in three pitches from Payton Tolle in the second.
As confirmed ahead of the postseason matchup , Max Fried will start on the mound as the Yankees go for the sweep.

articles.title_zh: ASU hockey coach is put on leave; hospitalized player is unlikely to recover, family attorney says
articles.content_orig:
Arizona State University has placed its hockey coach, Greg Powers, on paid administrative leave after a player collapsed during a workout last month and remains hospitalized.
ASU said assistant coach Mike Corbett will take over for now and that an interim coach would be named "soon." The school did not say how long Powers was expected to remain on leave.
Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old sophomore from Ontario, Canada, collapsed during a workout on Aug. 20. Robert Carey, an attorney for the Mayich family, has said he is "unlikely to recover," according to CBS affiliate KPHO-TV .
According to a report from the school about the incident, Mayich was taking part in a "wind-down" exercise that involved running with a medicine ball at one of the school's outdoor facilities when he collapsed. The high temperature that day was over 100 degrees, according to the National Weather Service, although the school said the workout took place when the temperature ranged from 86 to 89 degrees.
"When running, Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball, and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," the report said. Mayich was told to stay down by players and coaches and an athletic trainer tried to use iced towels and cold water to cool him down.
The school said Mayich was initially responsive but that his condition deteriorated.
Mayich's parents, John and Christina, had previously called for the coaches who ran the workout to be put on leave. In a statement Wednesday, they said putting only Powers on leave isn't enough.
"Putting Powers on leave while his best friend of the last decade stays in charge of the locker room doesn't solve the problem," they said in a statement. "If ASU won't remove him, even just to err on the side of player safety, then the interim head coach it has promised should have the authority to place on leave anyone who poses a risk of retaliation against these players."
Seven other players have disputed the school's version of events, saying in a letter sent Tuesday to ASU's president that the outside consultant who ran the workout was not approved in accordance with the school's policy, the workout lasted longer than the school said, the players did not receive sufficient water breaks, and the workout "continued after some of us showed signs of distress."
The students, who chose to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, stated that Mayich in particular was not given any water breaks and had shown signs of distress before the final exercise during which he collapsed. They also said required emergency equipment, like cold-water immersion tubs, wasn't on the field.
The workout, which the students say was run by Tim Ziesel, a man whom the school described as "an individual who had spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," was described in the students' letter as "grueling" and "military-style."
Ziesel, in a statement released by his attorney, said, "There is no such thing as a military style workout other than calisthenics done to a cadence."
"The term 'military style workout' is a term that was made up out of thin air," he said. "The actual workout would be considered easy by a high school varsity football or basketball team. I am a Navy Veteran and I was a head varsity coach for 28 years. The emphasis should be on [the] family of Matthew. They are not served by made up terms."
The students alleged Mayich was left in the sun for several minutes after he collapsed, and "the only cooling on hand was one small cooler holding a few Powerade sideline towels ... squirt bottles that put out a stream of water rather than a spray, and later, after he was moved, a garden hose with warm water."
The students in their letter requested that the staff responsible for the workout be placed on leave pending the results of an independent investigation.
Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell said Tuesday on social media that the ASU Police Department is investigating the incident, and once that probe is finished, her office will "review this matter at the highest level."

articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.content_orig:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.
“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”
The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.
“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”
Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.
Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.
“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.
“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.
He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
after newsletter promotion
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.
The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec .
The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.
The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 dips, Nasdaq higher after data shows moderate inflation rise
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 dips, Nasdaq higher after data shows moderate inflation rise
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields wavered as traders weighed lighter-than-expected U.S. inflation data for August as they awaited the September jobs report due later in the week.
The 2-year Treasury note yield was last little changed at 4.895%, while the 10-year Treasury yield was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.298%, recovering after a brief pullback earlier in the session. The benchmark yield traded near 2007 highs. The 30-year Treasury bond was up nearly 4 basis points at 5.632%, or around its highest level since 2002.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Consumer prices were reported Wednesday to have posted a smaller-than-expected increase in August compared to the same period a year ago, according to the Federal Reserve's primary measure of inflation.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.3% last month, putting the 12-month gain at 3.4%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for increases of 0.3% and 3.7% respectively.
"Net, net, the inflation fire is not burning as hot as markets expected in August, and bond yields are adjusting their sails as investors rethink exactly how many Fed rate hikes might be needed to keep inflation moving back down to target," Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, wrote in response to the latest release.
Excluding food and energy, PCE posted a 0.2% increase in August that put the annual core level at 3%. The respective forecasts were for 0.3% and 3.3%.
Though the Fed officially follows the headline PCE number, officials generally consider the core reading a better gauge of longer-term inflation trends.
The good news on inflation Wednesday came after recent commentary from Federal Reserve officials led to a repricing of monetary policy expectations. At one point this month, traders priced in a more than 80% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in October. Those odds sat around 37% after Wednesday's release, with traders pushing the next expected increase to December, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Yields initially moved lower on the data, though they turned back higher as traders began looking ahead to the September U.S. jobs report, due Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET. Economists expect the economy added 84,000 jobs this month.
If Friday's numbers come in hotter than expected — as did Wednesday's ADP private payrolls report — it could send yields higher.

Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.
On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.
Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).
Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa .
“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”
The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.
“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.
“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.
In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).
Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.
The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.
“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”
Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the state department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.
A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.
A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.
One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.
And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.
The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

Published: 09:41 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 10:14 EDT, 30 September 2026
The cousin of the murdered transgender New York Times executive gave his theory on a possible motive after he was allegedly gunned down by his in-laws.
Jonathan McKinsey, 40, was shot multiple times and killed in a parking lot at Dublin Sports Grounds in Dublin, California , on Saturday.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, were arrested on multiple charges, including murder, after police say they took turns shooting him.
McKinsey, the head of engineering for games player experience at the New York Times since 2023, was locked in a bitter custody battle with his estranged wife Candice Jang, Zhang and Chen's daughter.
Lovell Garner, McKinsey's cousin, was asked by the California Post if he believed that the in-laws were driven to support his wife's custody bid.
'I'd lay a lot of money on that,' Garner told the outlet. 'It's unbelievable that they would put themselves on the line like that for her.'
The cousin was still rattled by the news of McKinsey's death while speaking to the outlet.
'Well, it's all still pretty fresh for me, still. So far, everyone in my immediate family is completely shocked,' Garner said.
Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the head of engineering for games at the New York Times, suffered multiple gunshot wounds in a parking lot in Dublin, California, on Saturday
McKinsey's in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, are accused of fatally shooting him
'It seems obvious that they were done with him since they killed him. Not sure what would make them do something that extreme.'
Garner explained that he lost contact with his cousin for several years and reached out to him a year ago after hearing that he was going through a rough patch.
He described McKinsey as a 'very smart' and 'outgoing' person but added that he remembered his cousin more from before his transition.
The executive was previously known as Dawn Finney before he transitioned in 2010, according to the Post.
He married Jang in 2011, and they were together until December 2025, when Jang filed for divorce.
That same year, she filed a domestic violence prevention order against her spouse.
The wife accused him of physically, verbally and emotionally abusing her and their three young children, according to the protection order filed in Alameda County Court in October 2025 and obtained by the San Francisco Chronicle .
She claimed she suffered abuse at McKinsey's hands over a 17-year period and detailed more than a dozen alleged attacks between November 2020 and July 2025 alone.
Lovell Garner, McKinsey's cousin, told the California Post he would 'lay a lot of money on' the in-laws being driven to allegedly kill the executive to support his wife's custody bid
A protection order was granted by the judge, records show.
McKinsey was charged with cruelty to a child by endangering health and corporal injury to a child, both misdemeanors, and was freed on $50,000 bail.
At the time of his murder, he had also been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, which would have resulted in the charges being dropped upon completion, according to the Mercury News .
But McKinsey claimed in his own court filings that Jang was the one who had been abusive for more than 15 years.
In 2013, he claimed she beat him with a frying pan, according to the court documents. He also accused Jang of verbally denigrating the children.
He alleged that Chen, Jang's mother, was verbally abusive to one of the couple's young children, raising objections over the child's clothing.
McKinsey further accused his in-laws of making derogatory remarks about his gender transition.
He claimed Chen directed anti-LGBTQ+ slurs at him and the child, referring first to the child and then to McKinsey as a 'disgusting queer' and a 'pervert.'
McKinsey had worked in games tech for the New York Times since 2023

Witnesses said the elderly couple walked calmly away from the scene of the shooting, and they were arrested after being tracked to a black sedan (above) at a nearby intersection
The executive further accused Jang of being abusive during medical procedures related to his transition, claiming that at one point she tried to pull medical tubes from his body shortly after he had his breasts removed, according to the Mercury News.
He also alleged that Jang's father, who was not named in the filing, punched him in the chest while he was recovering from the double mastectomy.
On the day of McKinsey's death, witnesses reported seeing two masked shooters approach McKinsey in the parking lot and take turns unloading a barrage of shots into him before they 'calmly' walked away.
Images showed the suspects being taken into custody by the side of the road after they were reportedly flagged down by stunned witnesses to a nearby police sergeant.
Zhang and Chen have since been booked into Alameda County's Santa Rita Jail and are being held without bail on charges including murder, felony conspiracy, child endangerment and dangerously firing a gun.
Zhang and Chen's arraignment has been scheduled for Wednesday.
