articles.title_orig: UK ends 'one in, one out' migrant returns deal with France
articles.title_zh: UK ends 'one in, one out' migrant returns deal with France
articles.content_orig:
The UK's Home Office said on Wednesday that its year-old deal with France to return migrants crossing the Channel on small boats had ended.
"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the Home Office said, confirming the end of the so-called "one in, one out" deal, which was launched in August last year and was due to expire on Thursday.
The scheme, known as Operation Hillmore, was part of efforts by London and Paris to tackle illegal migration across the English Channel.
Under the arrangement, Britain could return to France some migrants who arrived illegally by small boat and were judged to have no right to remain in the UK. In exchange, Britain accepted an equal number of asylum seekers from France considered likely to qualify for protection, with priority given to vulnerable nationalities and people with family or other links to the UK.
The two countries agreed in June to extend the pilot until 1 October. The most recent Home Office figures show that 1,087 people were returned to France between 4 August 2025 and 30 June 2026, while 1,117 were transferred to the UK under the scheme. Over the same period, 27,920 migrants arrived in the UK on small boats, meaning only about 4% of arrivals were sent back.
That was one of the clearest signs of the programme's limited impact, despite government claims that it would deter people-smuggling gangs.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told MPs on 15 September that it cost the UK taxpayer an average of about £56,000 (€65,500) per migrant to return them.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, said that Brexit had made stopping small boats harder because the UK no longer had the same level of cooperation with the EU. He declined to set a date for ending the crossings, but told the BBC he and Mahmood would not stop until they had cracked down on "every element of this criminal, illegal activity".
Burnham has said his government is "changing the whole approach" to small boats, pairing tougher enforcement with safe legal routes for asylum seekers, which he argues would take away the smuggling gangs' main selling point.
France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in June that France wanted a more European approach to illegal migration . He also argued that France should not have to bear sole responsibility for policing an EU external border, blaming weak controls in countries of first entry and onward movement within the Schengen area.
Migrants trying to reach Britain pay smugglers thousands of euros for places on overcrowded inflatable boats to cross one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. Research has also shown a sharp rise this year in small boats setting off from Belgium, as smuggling networks look for new launch points.
Overall, some 197,000 people have crossed the Channel in small boats since the route emerged as a major migration pathway.

Apple ( AAPL ) stock rose in early trading on Wednesday following a report that the company is preparing to host an event next month outlining its entry into the smart home space.
According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman , Apple will unveil an all-new smart home hub designed to control devices throughout the home, serve as a digital calendar and reminder list, play music, make video calls, and more.
Shares of Apple rose nearly 3%.
The hub, which can be mounted on a wall or placed on a counter with an accompanying stand, is designed to recognize users and provide them with personalized content via voice or facial recognition. It will also take advantage of Apple's new Siri AI platform, which it launched in beta earlier this month.
Apple is also working on a secondary version of the smart home hub featuring a robotic arm that lets the screen rotate 360 degrees.
The home hub would stand as the first new product category for Apple under CEO John Ternus , though the project has been in the works for some time. It could also serve as a lucrative new revenue stream for the company if it catches on.
Current do-it-yourself hub-style solutions require users to mount iPads to their walls to control smart home products or access them via their iPhones.
In addition to the hub, Apple is also rolling out new versions of its Apple TV set-top box and HomePod mini smart speaker. Both devices will look roughly the same as their existing versions, though they'll get more powerful processors to run Siri AI.
According to Gurman , Apple is looking to speed up its product development by making the company leaner via layoffs and other reductions.
Apple is entering a market traditionally dominated by Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which had early success in the smart home space thanks to their Alexa and Google Assistant platforms, respectively.
The company's home offerings fall under its Wearables, Home, and Accessories segment, which brought in $35.68 billion in 2025, making it Apple's third-largest segment behind the iPhone and Services.

articles.title_orig: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.title_zh: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Tom Cruise has built a career on jumping out of airplanes, scaling skyscrapers and performing other high-wire antics in the name of entertainment. His next stunt may be his riskiest yet: Getting moviegoers to see “ Digger ,” a rare big-budget, star-driven R-rated original comedy.
The Warner Bros. release, which opens on Oct. 2, represents one of the fall season’s biggest gambles. There’s pressure on “Digger” not just to offset the studio’s terrible year at the box office (with bombs including Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s “Supergirl”) but also to impress the new corporate ownership. Paramount Skydance hopes to imminently close its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
It might not be Digger Rockwell to the rescue. “Digger,” directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu and starring an unrecognizable Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon whose company sparks an ecological calamity, is tracking a hugely disappointing launch of $12 million to $15 million in North America. Projections were at $18 million to $20 million but were revised down in recent days.
The film was greenlit at $125 million, but according to four knowledgable sources, the budget climbed to $160 million to $180 million after production went over schedule. A Warner Bros. spokesperson disputes those figures. Regardless, a movie of this size would need a debut near $40 million to justify its budget, per rival execs. Since exhibitors keep about half of ticket sales, and the studio spent another $100 million on marketing, “Digger” has a theatrical break-even point of roughly $350 million globally, according to executives with knowledge of similar films. A Warner Bros. spokesperson pushed back, saying the film’s break-even point is $300 million.
Reviews and word of mouth will factor into the film’s box office longevity, analysts say. They also note that “Digger” could be bigger overseas, where Cruise’s movies tend to make the bulk of their money. Profitability for WB may take longer because Cruise gets first-dollar gross, meaning he earns a percentage of revenues before the studio recoups any costs.
“Kudos to Warner Bros. for taking a chance; Tom Cruise has earned that right,” says analyst Jeff Bock of Exhibitor Relations. “But let’s be honest about where Tom Cruise is today. He’s a franchise machine. Can audiences accept him as a transformative actor again after he’s branded himself as the action hero?”
“Digger” is Cruise’s first original movie since 2017’s hit “American Made.” (That year, he also starred in the notorious flop “The Mummy.”) A bankable draw since the ‘80s, Cruise became synonymous with action stardom through the enduring “Mission: Impossible” franchise and then endeared himself to younger generations with 2022’s blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick.” But even Cruise has learned the hard way that moviegoers have become pickier about what’s worth getting off the couch for. His final two “Mission: Impossible” films — 2023’s “Dead Reckoning” and 2025’s “The Final Reckoning” — faced diminishing returns at the box office.
Cruise, an elusive star who doesn’t talk to press, has worked aggressively — if selectively — to sell “Digger.” Amid his global promotional tour, he made a rare podcast appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” and sat for his first cover story in two decades with GQ magazine — which raised eyebrows because the actor managed to avoid any personal questions and relentlessly directed the conversation back to his passion for movies.
“It takes a herculean effort to get word-of-mouth going for a black comedy,” says Bock. “Tom knows he has to go the extra mile with this film. His name alone isn’t going to sell it.”
Beyond Cruise’s star power, Warner Bros. co-chairs Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca were willing to spend big on “Digger” because Iñárritu, too, has a strong commercial track record. His 2015 film “The Revenant” generated $533 million globally and earned Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor Oscar. And 2014’s “Birdman” grossed $103 million against an $18 million budget and won best picture. Iñárritu hasn’t released a film theatrically in more than a decade; his last movie, the polarizing drama “Bardo, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths,” was set at Netflix.
“The combination of an accomplished auteur and a top star has resulted in some very interesting and successful pictures,” says analyst David A. Gross of Franchise Re, citing examples like “One Battle After Another” with DiCaprio and director Paul Thomas Anderson and “F1” with Brad Pitt and director Joseph Kosinski. “But the movie has to connect and satisfy broad tastes. If word-of-mouth is poor, the film is going to struggle.”
Abdy and De Luca, known for their taste and talent relations, faced similar scrutiny ahead of last year’s “One Battle After Another” — another expensive, auteurist swing. That film opened to $22 million and climbed to $213 million globally. Although an impressive result for a nearly three-hour original comedic drama, those returns weren’t enough to get the movie out of the red. “One Battle” lost $100 million theatrically. It did, however, prove valuable in other ways — namely, winning the best picture Oscar.
Moreover, Warner Bros. could withstand the major write-down because it was riding high on a massive year at the box office. The studio had fielded an unprecedented run of profitable hits , including “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie,” “Weapons” and “Final Destination: Bloodlines.” In 2025, the company had seven movies that grossed $100 million domestically and commanded 21% of the North American box office.
Fast forward a year, and Warner Bros. isn’t in the same shape. The studio has yet to release a single film that grossed $100 million domestically, and commands just 6% of the domestic market. That’s while the box office is enjoying its biggest year since the onset of COVID , fueled by the best summer season ever recorded.
For all the eyes on Warner Bros. as the studio braces for new leadership, Paramount isn’t having much better a year. Despite profitable releases like “Scary Movie” and “Scream,” Paramount ranks seventh among studios with just 5% of the domestic marketshare.
Warners is expected to rebound with December’s “Dune: Part III.” The third entry in Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi franchise, starring Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, is shaping up to be the highest-grossing installment in the series.
But before returning to the desert planet of Arrakis, the studio has to mop up a lot of red ink. “The Bride!” will lose $100 million theatrically after collapsing with $24 million worldwide against a $90 million budget. “Supergirl” tapped out with $126 million globally against a $170 million budget, and will lose $80 million. “The End of Oak Street,” a sci-fi adventure starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, has grossed $121 million worldwide against an $85 million budget, putting estimated theatrical losses between $25 million and $40 million. “Practical Magic 2,” a legacy sequel that brought back Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock as witchy sisters, is running out of steam with $92 million globally against a $75 million budget; it could lose around $30 million to $40 million in its theatrical run.
